newsitem.title: BELGIUM: OLOs lie low after early rally,more gains expected.
newsitem.headline: OLOs lie low after early rally,more gains expected.

text.p: Belgian government bonds (OLOs) and futures paused after strong gains on Wednesday morning, but dealers were optimistic the market had scope for further gains.
News from the U.S. that the economy's growth was slowing and inflation in 1997 would be quite modest, underpinned prices.
The comments, from U.S. Fed chairman Alan Greenspan, were taken as signs that U.S. rate hikes were not likely for now.

The pause from the morning's rally came amid talk that the Bundesbank was mulling a variable rate repo tender or a small hike on official rates to slow the mark's losses on the dollar on the back of the bullish Greenspan remarks.
Given the close link between the mark and the franc a German interest rate rise would most probably be followed by the Belgian National bank.

The dollar pressure also affected the franc, in turn driving short Belgian rates higher. One-week repo rates were at 3.85/91 percent late on Wednesday, above this morning's 3.65/70, and far above the central bank's three percent central rate.

But dealers said the rates were moving purely with German rates, leaving the short spread at around 20 basis points. "That is enough as far as the franc is concerned...any insecurity in the Belgian market is discounted," one trader said.
The franc slipped to 20.6490/95 to the mark from 20.6445/60 late on Tuesday.
Demand for the longer end helped the 10-year OLO/Bund spread narrow a tick to seven basis points from eight. The yield on the benchmark 10-year OLO BE286= eased to 5.57 percent from 5.61.

One trader said 5.50 percent yields were still likely despite the drying-up of action in the wake of the Bundesbank talk. Having turned more cautious, he said the threshold would be crossed by year-end at the latest. He noted that while for now there seemed little chance of higher U.S. rates, the U.S. and European cycles were at different stages.
"We should not be discounting the news from the States in full," he said.

Other dealers and analysts said OLOs would head for a test of February's all-time highs following Greenspan's reassuring remarks on inflation and growth. The 10-year OLO yield hit 5.50 percent on February 18.
Any late summer gains could, however, be capped by the prospect of higher European growth, they added.
Talk of a weak Euro, which has pushed the dollar and other non-EMU currencies higher against the mark DEM=, was not yet a factor for hard-core European bonds.
Kredietbank economist Conrad Fieremans said the bond market had so far ignored the sell-off in the mark and this was not likely to change soon.
This year's collapse in the spread between Treasuries and Bunds MEUR from around 120 to 70 basis points was mainly due to the difference in the U.S. and German economic cycles.
"The question is what happens in the third quarter. We expect strong economies both in the U.S. and Europe," Fieremans said.
